messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: Citation text (authors, title, journal, year, article number) matches the information in the provided source metadata.
DOI URL exactly matches the DOI given in the source metadata (10.1016/j.jwpe.2025.107875).

The source states that adsorption experiments used deionized water spiked with a mixture of PFAS and Cd(II) at 10 mg/L each (S05-E06). The PFAS identities (PFOA, PFOS, GenX) are confirmed elsewhere (S05-E02, S05-E05). The phrase about subsequent acid regeneration is consistent with the regeneration section (S05-E05, S05-E08).
PFOA, PFOS, and GenX are explicitly listed as the PFAS mixture components (S05-E02, S05-E05, S05-E06).
PFOA, PFOS, and GenX are explicitly listed as the PFAS mixture components (S05-E02, S05-E05, S05-E06).
PFOA, PFOS, and GenX are explicitly listed as the PFAS mixture components (S05-E02, S05-E05, S05-E06).
Activated carbon (AC) and wood-derived biochar (BC-W) are identified as the selected adsorbents for detailed evaluation and regeneration (S05-E01, S05-E02).
The initial concentration of each PFOA, PFOS, and GenX was 10 mg L−1 (S05-E02, S05-E05). The numeric value 10 matches this.
The unit mg L−1 is explicitly given for each PFAS (S05-E02, S05-E05).
The initial concentration of Cd(II) is reported as 10 mg L−1 (S05-E02).
The unit mg L−1 is explicitly given for Cd(II) (S05-E02).
Batch adsorption used 20 mg adsorbent in 20 mL solution (S05-E06), which equals 1 g L−1; this matches the reported value.
The dose is described as 1 g L−1 of adsorbent (S05-E06), matching the unit.
Both the adsorption and the initial loading before regeneration were conducted for 24 h (S05-E05, S05-E06).
Contact time is explicitly given in hours (24 h) (S05-E05, S05-E06).
Regeneration strategies include treatment with 0.1 M HCl solution among the eluants (S05-E05, S05-E08). The value correctly names this regenerant.
The protocol states that 100 mg adsorbent was treated with 5 mL of eluant for regeneration (S05-E05), matching the numeric value 5 mL per 100 mg adsorbent.
The regeneration eluant volume is explicitly given in milliliters (5 mL) (S05-E05).
The regeneration step involved treating adsorbents with eluants for another 24 h (S05-E05).
Regeneration contact time is explicitly 24 h (S05-E05), so the unit hours is correct.

Regeneration is described as conducted at room temperature (S05-E05); adsorption experiments are separately given as 24 ± 2 °C (S05-E06). Representing regeneration temperature numerically as ~24 °C is reasonable but not directly quantified for regeneration, so the approximate numeric value is inferred rather than explicitly stated.
Temperature is discussed in °C for adsorption (24 ± 2 °C, S05-E06), and regeneration is said to be at room temperature (S05-E05). Using °C as the unit is appropriate.
The text notes that three adsorption–desorption cycles were conducted for reuse ("three adsorption-desorption cycles" in S05-E08 and "Three adsorption-" in S05-E05), matching the reported value of 3.

This endpoint describes desorption of Cd(II) into the HCl regenerant. The source states that the HCl solution removed Cd(II) (S05-E08), which is a phase separation process (from solid adsorbent to liquid regenerant), so classification as a separation endpoint is appropriate.

This endpoint concerns PFAS desorption into the regenerant. The source notes that HCl showed limited efficiency in removing PFAS (S05-E08), again indicating transfer from solid to liquid phase; classification as separation is appropriate.

This endpoint concerns removal of PFAS and Cd(II) from solution by regenerated adsorbents over cycles. The source states that adsorbents maintained >90% of their adsorption performance for both PFAS and Cd(II) over three cycles (S05-E08), which is a removal-from-solution outcome, so endpoint_type=removal is appropriate.

Regeneration text reports HCl removed Cd(II) but had limited PFAS removal (S05-E08) and does not provide explicit numerical percentages for these HCl desorption efficiencies; the limitation that only qualitative descriptions are provided is a reasonable design inference consistent with the cited text.

Regeneration was done in batch at room temperature (S05-E05, S05-E08) starting from defined PFAS/Cd(II) mixtures (S05-E02), and reuse is described for three adsorption-desorption cycles (S05-E05, S05-E08). The limitation that experiments are limited to batch tests with this mixture and up to three cycles is a necessary design inference from these details.

The source states that both adsorbents were capable of maintaining >90% of their adsorption performance for both PFAS and Cd(II) for three adsorption-desorption cycles (S05-E08). The recorded value ">90" with inequality form matches this statement.
The phrase ">90% of their adsorption performance" (S05-E08) implies percent; the unit % is correct.

The >90% retention over three cycles for both PFAS and Cd(II) is explicitly supported (S05-E08). However, the qualifier that this occurs "across the regeneration strategies tested (including acid)" is not explicitly stated; the text does not break down performance by individual regenerant. Thus, the core quantitative statement is supported but the scope over all strategies is inferred.

HCl solution is reported to remove Cd(II) (S05-E08), and the paper notes that desorbed Cd(II) can be concentrated and extracted using established metal recovery techniques (S05-E01). It is therefore supported that the acid regeneration stream contains elevated Cd(II) suitable for potential metal recovery.

The text states that HCl removed Cd(II) but showed limited efficiency in removing PFAS (S05-E08). It follows necessarily that some PFAS remains adsorbed on the media after single-step HCl regeneration, even though this is not spelled out verbatim.

Experiments use mg quantities of adsorbent in mL-scale batch bottles (20 mg in 20 mL, 100 mg in 100 mL) (S05-E05, S05-E06), clearly indicating bench-scale batch regeneration tests with AC and BC-W and 0.1 M HCl among the eluants.

The methods describe regeneration of PFAS- and Cd(II)-loaded AC and BC-W using 0.1 M HCl (among other eluants) followed by reuse in further adsorption cycles (S05-E05, S05-E08). Focusing this treatment description on the single-step HCl regeneration plus reuse is consistent with those details.

All regeneration strategies (methanol, HCl, sequential methanol/HCl) use the same adsorbents, initial solute concentrations (10 mg/L each PFAS and Cd(II)), and adsorbent dose (1 g/L) in batch at room temperature (S05-E02, S05-E05, S05-E08). It is a reasonable inference that these experiments are comparable with conditions across regenerants.

The stated reason—that HCl regeneration experiments share adsorbents, mixture, loading conditions, and batch setup with the other strategies—is directly supported by the common experimental setup for regeneration tests (S05-E02, S05-E05, S05-E08).

result.record_usable_rationale: Core elements—source identity, matrix, PFAS compounds, adsorbents, regeneration conditions (0.1 M HCl), number of cycles, and the main quantitative finding (>90% performance retention over three cycles)—are directly supported by the cited text. Minor issues are limited to qualifiers (e.g., extrapolating performance across all regenerants or approximating room temperature as ~24 °C) and do not materially misrepresent the study or impede its use in synthesis.
